source.title: Scaling Analysis of Interleaved Speech-Text Language Models
source.authors: Gallil Maimon; Michael Hassid; Amit Roth; Yossi Adi

record.tranche_reason: Applies fixed-compute model-size scaling analysis to interleaved speech-text language models, a new training regime, and reports speech validation loss and downstream metrics.
record.gate_note: The study measures speech-only validation cross-entropy across model sizes and compute budgets, and fits downstream metric trends against compute. Its plots also include task metrics and comparisons with speech-only training and different initialisations; only results bearing on the listed scaling versions are recorded. Prior-work estimates shown for comparison are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study runs its own fixed-compute model-size sweeps (ISO-FLOP style) for interleaved speech-text SLMs initialised from Qwen2.5. This is a new modality and continued-training regime. It reports where the best size lies per budget and fits power laws of semantic speech metrics against compute, which bears on V3, V6 and V7. It fits no loss power law and checks no extrapolation, so V1, V2 and V5 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that interleaved SLMs initialised from strong TextLMs scale more efficiently with compute than textless SLMs, with better semantic performance per compute and a steeper sSC slope. They conclude far more compute should go to parameters than tokens. They caution that sweep granularity is limited, the best model may be off-optimal, and the results are hard to extrapolate.
record.recipe_differences: Uses fixed-compute model-size sweeps inspired by ISO-FLOP analysis, but applies them to interleaved speech-text SLMs initialized from pretrained TextLMs and evaluates speech validation loss plus semantic speech tasks.
record.method_sensitivity: Model family and TextLM initialisation affect results; synthetic versus real speech data also changes validation and task performance. The study says some smaller or weaker TextLMs benefit less from interleaving.

fits_no_version.finding: The effect of text initialisation decays with training tokens: the loss gap to from-scratch narrows, while the task-metric gap persists. The authors hypothesise this changes the D-dependence of the scaling form.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initialisation from a pretrained model alters the token-scaling term of continued-pretraining loss.

record.problems: The authors state that existing pretrained model sizes limit sweep granularity and make low-compute analysis difficult, and that the best model may be away from the true optimum. Figure 4 loss values are plotted rather than tabulated; no uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: Figure 4 points are recorded individually for speech-only validation cross-entropy. Figure 1 comparator equations for textless SLMs and TextLMs are estimates from Cuervo & Marxer (2024), not this study's own results, so they are not rows. Other training-regime comparisons are not fitted scaling-law results.

untested.parts: No power-law fit of held-out loss in N, D or C. The authors say a functional form is challenging to fit in this regime.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs. The authors say the results are hard to extrapolate.
No exponents for optimal N and D versus compute. Granularity is limited to four pretrained sizes.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No loss power-law form is fitted for the speech/interleaved regime. Only downstream-metric power laws are fitted.
Only semantic StoryCloze metrics are fitted. sBLIMP and cross-modal tasks are not fitted against compute.

missing.what: Validation CE versus semantic metrics across real, synthetic and mixed data. Lower loss does not mean better semantic accuracy.
Fixed-compute size sweep for MS-sSC, described by the authors as noisier, with trends similar to loss.
Fixed-compute size sweep for multi-speaker tSC, on which r21's allocation statement rests.

record.verdict_notes: The regime is continued training from pretrained text LMs into speech, not from-scratch pretraining, so V3/V7 evidence concerns this setting. Compute counts only SLM training, not TextLM pretraining. Learning rates were changed for budgets ≥2e20 and tuned per model at 6e19, which may affect the sweep. Figure 1 comparator equations for SLM and TLM are from Cuervo & Marxer and are correctly excluded as rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study plots speech-only validation loss over model-size and compute-budget sweeps, but does not fit or establish a power law for held-out loss, isolate parameter/token/compute scaling with the other variables non-bottleneck, or demonstrate several orders of magnitude.
No small-run fit is evaluated as a prediction of much larger runs.

The study compares sizes at fixed compute and discusses allocation trends, but does not estimate stable power exponents for optimal parameter and token counts versus compute. It does not establish both counts' growth rates.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study analyzes an interleaved speech-text regime but does not test whether the same held-out-loss power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
The study fits selected semantic speech metrics against compute; it does not test predictability across a broad range of downstream tasks or from pretraining loss.

The study reports sensitivity to model family, data, and initialisation in performance, but does not test whether fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal split estimates depend on these choices, or whether curves bend from a single power law.

rows.subject: SIMS interleaved SLM size sweep (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compare model sizes at fixed compute and infer allocation trend

conditions.value: compute ≤ 5e18 FLOPs and larger budgets, including 2e20 FLOPs

rows.measure: Compute-optimal model-size allocation, using speech-only validation loss and semantic metrics
rows.value: The authors say they cannot identify the exact ideal model size per curve; for semantic metrics the smallest model is best at compute ≤ 5e18 FLOPs, while larger models are better beyond that; at 2e20 FLOPs the 7B model is reported as best by a large margin.
rows.note: Aggregate interpretation of the size sweep; the paper does not give a fitted optimal-size power law.
rows.check: Add V7. The optimum shifts to larger models with compute: smallest best at ≤5e18; 7B on 4.2B tokens best at 2e20. That split is far more parameter-heavy than the Chinchilla ratio or the textless-SLM estimate (463M on 72B tokens). No optimal-N/D exponents are fitted. The 'smallest model best' statement refers to semantic metrics.

source_check.correct: V3: cannot_determine; stable compute-allocation powers are not established. V7: observed; the allocation differs from the textless-SLM estimate. The smallest model is best on semantic metrics at compute ≤5e18 FLOPs; at 2e20 FLOPs, the best tested model has 7B parameters and 4.2B training tokens.
source_check.locator_found: Section 5, Figure 4 and accompanying discussion, pp. 7–8.
source_check.problem: A shared partial state conflates untested stable allocation powers with observed setup dependence.

relationships.condition: Interleaved speech-text SLMs initialised from pretrained Qwen2.5, budgets 2.1e18–2e20 FLOPs
relationships.reason: r21: the best size per budget is far more parameter-heavy than equal N/D growth (7B on 4.2B tokens at 2e20). The authors tie this to text initialisation. No stable exponents are fitted.
relationships.display_finding: At 2e20 FLOPs, the best tested configuration used 7B parameters and 4.2B tokens, a parameter-heavy allocation attributed to text initialization.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Interleaved speech-text SLMs initialised from pretrained Qwen2.5, budgets 2.1e18–2e20 FLOPs
source_check.reason: r21 establishes a parameter-heavy allocation among tested sizes, but neither fits stable allocation powers nor demonstrates their failure. A different allocation ratio does not establish unequal growth exponents. Untested stability cannot justify limits_scope.

relationships.condition: Interleaved text-initialised SLMs vs textless-SLM scaling estimates
relationships.reason: r21: the compute-optimal split differs sharply from the textless-SLM law (7B/4.2B vs 463M/72B tokens at 2e20). The comparator values come from Cuervo & Marxer.
relationships.display_finding: At 2e20 FLOPs, the optimal allocation was 7B parameters and 4.2B tokens, versus 463M parameters and 72B tokens under Cuervo and Marxer's textless-model estimates.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Interleaved text-initialised SLMs vs textless-SLM scaling estimates
source_check.reason: Section 5 reports 7B parameters/4.2B tokens as best tested at 2e20 FLOPs, versus the cited textless-SLM recommendation of 463M/72B, supporting setup-dependent allocation.

relationships.condition: Semantic speech metrics (sSC, tSC, multi-speaker variants) at best size per compute, ~2e18–7e20 FLOPs
relationships.reason: r22–r25: each metric is fitted as a power law in compute with small positive exponents (0.018–0.026). No fit quality is reported.
relationships.display_finding: Each semantic speech metric was fitted by a compute power law with positive exponents of 0.018–0.026, without reported fit quality.

source_check.reason: Figure 1 gives positive compute power-law exponents: sSC 0.026, tSC 0.018, multi-speaker sSC 0.020 and multi-speaker tSC 0.021. Section 5 cautions about noise and restricted model sizes.

relationships.condition: Predicting downstream performance from speech validation loss across training-data mixes (Qwen2.5-0.5B, 20k steps)
relationships.reason: Based on text (Table 1), no row. The real-only model has lower validation CE (1.961 vs 1.983) but worse sSC and MS-sSC than real+synthetic. The authors say loss may not reflect semantic performance.
relationships.display_finding: Real-only training achieved lower cross-entropy, 1.961 versus 1.983, but worse sSC and MS-sSC than training on real and synthetic speech.
